mediaItem.summaryNotes: This episode of "Wrongful Conviction with Maggie Freeling" tells the story of Patty Pruitt, wrongfully convicted of murdering her husband Bill in 1984.  The podcast details the flawed police investigation, highlighting how investigators quickly focused on Patty due to her past marital issues and ignored crucial evidence, including a potential rape Patty experienced the night of the murder and a neighbor's report of a suspicious vehicle. The prosecution used character assassination, focusing on Patty's past relationships to paint her as a bad wife and mother, which influenced the jury.  Key evidence was overlooked, and Patty's defense was weak, failing to present critical information. Despite later admissions of investigative flaws by the prosecutor himself and the potential for DNA evidence to support Patty's rape claim, she remains incarcerated, having served nearly 36 years, maintaining her innocence and becoming a mentor to other incarcerated women.

featuredIndividual.sentence: Life in prison with possibility of parole after 50 years
contributingFactorsRaw: Tunnel vision by police, flawed investigation, character assassination by prosecution (sexist tropes and gender bias), ineffective defense,  overlooked evidence,  community bias,  use of unreliable expert witness (pathologist).
organizationsInvolvedRaw: AIG Pro Bono Program (mentioned as underwriter, implying general support for justice reform), Patty's legal team (Brian Reichhardt mentioned).
innocenceLawyersRaw: Brian Reichhardt -  lawyer who encountered Patty's case in law school in 2010 and became convinced of wrongful conviction. Has been working on her case since.
featuredIndividual.crossReference: Not specified if in exoneree database within the transcript.
featuredIndividual.narrativeOriginalCrime: Patty Pruitt reported being awakened by an intruder who raped her, after which she found her husband Bill struggling to breathe and discovered he had been shot.
keyEvidenceProsecutionRaw: Life insurance policy on Bill naming Patty as beneficiary, Patty's past sexual relationships outside of marriage (presented as motive - greed and lust), Patty's collection of murder mystery novels,  recovered .22 caliber gun (presumed murder weapon), pathologist testimony.
featuredIndividual.trialDefenderNotes: Defense did not present expert to refute pathologist, did not highlight consensual nature of Patty's past relationships, did not bring up Patty's rape at trial (due to Patty's wishes to protect Bill's reputation and shield children). Seemed generally ineffective in countering prosecution's character assassination.
keyEvidenceExonerationRaw: Book by deceased prosecutor Tom Williams admitting to shoddy investigation and reliance on character attacks.  Uncovered pajamas potentially holding DNA evidence from the night of the murder and alleged rape (DNA testing requested but denied). Neighbor's ignored report of suspicious vehicle. Daughter's testimony about light in basement ignored.
featuredIndividual.actualPerpetratorDetails: Not identified in the podcast. Potential theories mentioned: involvement of drug trade in the community, unknown intruder.

keyQuotesRaw: Patty Pruitt: "I did not kill my husband."

Patty Pruitt (regarding her role in prison): "If I can't help people, what's the least again alive?" and "So the only way these kids are ever going to be somebody and get out of this endless loop of incarceration is to believe in themselves and realize that they're good people, and they deserve a good life."

Prosecutor Williams (in his book):  Admits to "shoddy investigation", criticizing his own star witness pathologist as a "doctor cop", and admitting to gratuitously attacking Patty's character to sway the jury.
Judge Kaufman (denying DNA testing): "you cannot believe her story and DNA findings of any kind do not change that fact."
systemicIssuesRaw: Tunnel vision in police investigations,  misogyny and gender bias in the justice system,  prosecutorial misconduct (character assassination, reliance on weak evidence), ineffective defense counsel,  impact of community bias and gossip,  difficulty of post-conviction relief even with new evidence.
policyRecommendationsRaw: Implied call for clemency for Patty Pruitt. General call to support innocence organizations.  Implicit need for police reform to prevent tunnel vision and biased investigations, and for prosecutorial reform to prevent character-based prosecutions.  Importance of DNA testing and re-examination of older cases.
personalNarrativeRaw: Patty Pruitt's wrongful conviction resulted in immense personal loss: loss of freedom for decades, loss of her role as a mother to her children during their formative years, inability to grieve with family during deaths of loved ones, and enduring the trauma of the wrongful accusation and imprisonment. Despite this, she has become a mentor and "mother figure" to many incarcerated women, demonstrating resilience and a commitment to helping others within a broken system.
